content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper examines the setting of online nonconvex-strongly-concave min-max optimization. To do so, they introduce a notion of dynamic regret for online nonconvex-strongly-concave min-max problem, which they call local Nash equilibrium (NE)-regret. In the case where the opponent is removed from the setting (e.g. the strategy set Y is a singleton) this notion reduces to the local regret proposed in Hazan et al.(2017). They propose an algorithm for this setting that they call time-Smoothed Online gradient Descent Ascent (SODA). At the high-level, their algorithm plays following the-leader iterates, while aiming to find a suitable approximating stationary point at each round using two-timescale gradient descent ascent. They provide an analysis of the local Nash regret showing that this method achieves local regret boundof O(T/w^2), taking O (Tw) iteration. These are exactly the same bounds as in Hazan et al and the optimality of these bounds follow from that work. They show an stochastic first-order feedback implementation of their algorithm achieving the same regret. Finally, they provide some experiments on training an empiricalWasserstein robustness model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1) The paper provides a new algorithm with tight theoretical analysis in a hard setting of online nonconvex-strongly-concave min-max problem.
2) The literature review seems thorough and up-to-date to me.


Weaknesses:
1) I believe that the paper readability should be improved. Just to point out one readability issue in the introduction in the our contribution section the authors describe their regret results as a function of parameter w but this parameter (as well as the formal definition of regret) is not given anywhere before that. I found myself jumping back and forth between this paper and Hazan et al to fill in some gaps.
2) The clear connections to Hazan et al. seems to lessen the impact of the contribution. 
3) The experimental section is relatively weak. Although on one hand, I understand the justification of the target solution concept as something for which positive guarantees can be proven in the worst case, however, the implementation section feels a little perfunctory. For example in the introduction the class of online nonconvex-strongly-concave min-max optimization is incentivized by the observation that time-varying two-player zero-sum stochastic games where the payoffs change with time, the policies are modeled by DNNs with strong regularization belong in this class. But in such settings there are a lot of strong benchmark algorithms to compete against. I believe such tests would be much more insightful.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As noted above I believe that the paper's readability is a pain point that needs to be addressed. The introduction is very vague both about what is the introduced solution concept as well as what are the main parameters used in the description of the key results of the paper (e.g. w). I think that the most natural way to introduce the paper is in the presence of the paper of Hazan et al, which is already in the rather relevant setting of non-convex games. Also, given that type of introduction, the authors could have pointed out more clearly which are the points of novelty introduced by them and to argue to what extent there were significantly additional technical hurdles in acquiring these results.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a largely theoretical paper for a hard setting of online min-max games. Although the provided guarantees are optimal, the relevance to prior work as well as the less than satisfactory writing style lessens the impact of the work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies online nonconvex-strongly-concave min-max problems with dynamic loss functions. The paper discusses the definition of local NE-Regret for online nonconvex-strongly-concave min-max problem and then proposes SODA for this setting. The paper also generalizes SODA to the setting with stochastic gradient feedback and proposes a stochastic variation of SODA. Both algorithms achieve a regret of $O(T/w^2)$.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

1. The theoretical results are sound and look rigorous. The presentation is clear and easy to read. 
2. This paper is the first one to study online nonconvex-strongly-concave min-max problem, which is novel.

Weaknesses

1. The paper looks not novel enough. The algorithm and analysis seem a combination of Lin et al. (2020a) and Hallak et al. (2021).
2. The experiments do not contain the results of SODA-SFO.
3. The online WRM model used in the experiments seems a bit artificial. It would be better if the authors could perform experiments on the applications introduced in the first section (such as the time-varying two-player zero-sum stochastic games).

Minors:

1. The figures in the experiments section are a bit small. I suggest the authors use a larger font size for the figures.
2. To increase the readability, Alg 2 should be presented in section 4 rather than the appendix.
3. The theoretical part should provide the optimal choice of $w$ and $\delta$.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is mostly clear. The theoretical results are solid, but the empirical results need to be improved.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the theoretical contribution is near the boardline, but the empirical part is below the bar.

content.title: Online Min-max Optimization: Nonconvexity, Nonstationarity, and Dynamic Regret
content.abstract: Online min-max optimization has recently gained considerable interest due to its rich applications to game theory, multi-agent reinforcement learning, online robust learning, etc. Theoretical understanding in this field has been mainly focused on convex-concave settings. Online min-max optimization with nonconvex geometries, which captures various online deep learning problems, has yet been studied so far. In this paper, we make the first  effort and investigate online nonconvex-strongly-concave min-max optimization in the nonstationary environment. We first introduce a natural notion of local Nash equilibrium (NE)-regret, and then propose a novel algorithm coined SODA to achieve the optimal regret. We further generalize our study to the setting with stochastic first-order feedback, and show that a variation of SODA can also achieve the same optimal regret in expectation. Our theoretical results and the superior performance of the proposed method are further validated by empirical experiments. To our best knowledge, this is the first exploration of efficient online nonconvex min-max optimization.
